Family Health

Bilirubin blood tests: jaundice, preparation and results

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A bilirubin test measures a yellow pigment made as red blood cells break down. It helps investigate jaundice and monitor treatment, but one result does not identify the cause or prove liver damage. Newborns need a different interpretation from adults. Do not postpone care for a yellow or unwell baby while arranging a routine test.

When jaundice needs urgent help

Get immediate emergency assessment for a jaundiced baby who is unusually sleepy or hard to wake, is not feeding, is floppy or stiff, has jerking movements, breathing difficulty, no wet nappies, or a temperature of 38°C or higher or 36°C or lower. Jaundice in the first 24 hours also needs immediate hospital assessment. Do not drive yourself with an unwell baby; arrange another driver or emergency transport.

After the first day, suspected or worsening jaundice, dark urine or pale creamy/chalky stools need urgent same-day advice even if the baby seems well. New yellow skin or eyes in an older child or adult also needs urgent medical assessment. Fatigue, itching, reduced appetite, dark urine or pale stools may accompany it. Severe abdominal pain with fever, confusion or collapse needs emergency care rather than waiting for a laboratory appointment.

Direct, indirect and total bilirubin

Normal breakdown of haemoglobin in older red cells produces bilirubin. Unconjugated, or indirect, bilirubin travels to the liver, largely attached to albumin. The liver joins it to glucuronic acid, making conjugated bilirubin more water-soluble for excretion into bile. Bile carries it through the bile ducts to the intestine; its breakdown products leave mainly in stool. The gallbladder stores bile, but not all bile must pass through it first.

Reports may list total bilirubin and a direct fraction, which broadly reflects conjugated bilirubin; indirect bilirubin is commonly calculated as total minus direct. These fractions help narrow the possibilities, not diagnose them alone. Bilirubin can rise because too much is produced, processing is altered, or bile drainage is impaired. A raised level is not automatically evidence of liver injury.

Why the test is requested

Testing can investigate yellow skin or eyes, suspected liver or bile-duct disease, excessive red-cell destruction called haemolysis, or a treatment response. In newborns, increased production and immature bilirubin handling commonly contribute to jaundice. That does not mean every baby has pathological haemolysis or that all jaundice is harmless.

Bilirubin may be part of a wider liver panel with ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase, albumin and total protein. These tests answer different questions; their pattern, symptoms, examination and previous results matter. Blood counts and other haemolysis tests, urine testing or ultrasound may be chosen. Not everyone needs every test, and a normal bilirubin result does not rule out every liver condition.

What happens during sampling

A trained professional usually takes a small sample from an arm vein into a collection tube. There may be a brief sting and mild aching afterwards. In newborns, a heel-prick sample is often used; a venous sample may sometimes be needed. Ask the team how they will support comfort during the procedure.

A skin bilirubin meter can estimate a newborn’s level without a needle, but it does not replace blood testing in every situation. Babies in their first 24 hours or born before 35 weeks of gestation need serum testing. High or near-treatment skin readings need confirmation according to the clinical protocol. Skin colour alone cannot establish the number or its safety.

Preparation: ask about food and medicines

Follow the ordering clinician’s or laboratory’s instructions; there is no universal four-hour fasting rule. Older patients may be asked to fast for particular tests taken together. Clarify how long, whether water is allowed, and what to do with diabetes treatment or fluid restrictions. Do not fast a newborn for a routine bilirubin check or withhold needed feeds while waiting.

Give the team a complete medicine and supplement list, including any penicillin G, phenobarbital, furosemide or theophylline you take. This is not a list of medicines to stop automatically. Furosemide is a diuretic, not a laxative. Medicines may affect results or bilirubin handling, but necessary treatment must not be stopped or altered without specific prescriber advice.

Risks and care after a blood test

Brief pain or a small bruise is common; faintness, a larger collection of blood under the skin called a haematoma, prolonged bleeding and infection are less common risks. Tell staff about previous fainting, bleeding problems, blood thinners and dressing allergies. Sit or lie down if lightheaded and alert the team.

Press on the sampling site as directed and follow local advice about the dressing and lifting or exercise; the same timing is not needed for everyone. Keep the area clean. Seek prompt medical advice for bleeding that persists despite firm pressure, a growing painful swelling or signs of infection. Heavy uncontrolled bleeding, collapse or severe symptoms require emergency help. Prolonged bleeding needs assessment but does not by itself prove a serious blood disorder.

Reading the result: age, units and trends

Use the reference interval printed by the laboratory. As an adult example, MedlinePlus lists total bilirubin around 0.1–1.2 mg/dL and direct bilirubin below 0.3 mg/dL; other laboratories differ. Reports may use µmol/L instead, so numbers cannot be compared without checking units. An isolated mild abnormality needs interpretation, not an assumed diagnosis or treatment.

Adult ranges and a fixed newborn cutoff such as 5.2 mg/dL do not determine neonatal safety. The team considers age in hours, gestational age, total serum bilirubin, the speed of change and risk factors such as haemolysis or illness, then uses the appropriate treatment chart. The same number can mean different things at different ages. Direct bilirubin should not be subtracted from total when applying neonatal treatment thresholds.

Possible causes in older children and adults

Raised bilirubin may accompany hepatitis, cirrhosis, medicine-related liver injury, Gilbert syndrome, gallstones or narrowed bile ducts. Pancreatic or gallbladder cancer is another possible cause of obstruction, but a high result is not a cancer diagnosis. Gilbert syndrome usually causes mild intermittent unconjugated elevation; it should not be guessed from a number without assessing other causes.

Haemolysis can raise indirect bilirubin without primary liver disease. Causes include autoimmune conditions, inherited red-cell disorders, infections, some medicines and reactions to a blood transfusion. A transfusion reaction is a specific clinical problem, not something a bilirubin result proves. Tell the treating team immediately about symptoms during or after a transfusion; they will assess the reaction and choose tests and treatment.

Newborn jaundice: different patterns and causes

Physiological jaundice commonly becomes noticeable after the first day as bilirubin production and clearance adjust. Suboptimal-intake jaundice often occurs in the first week when too little milk is transferred. Breast milk jaundice is a different pattern, usually in the second or later weeks, sometimes lasting longer in an otherwise thriving baby; its exact mechanism is uncertain. Persistent jaundice still needs assessment rather than assuming breast milk is the cause.

Other causes include blood-group antibody haemolysis, G6PD deficiency or other inherited red-cell/enzyme disorders, bruising, excess red cells called polycythaemia, infection and liver or bile-drainage disease. Prematurity increases vulnerability but does not itself mean polycythaemia. Sickle cell disease can cause haemolysis later in life but is not a usual explanation for jaundice in the first newborn days; symptoms generally begin months later. Maternal and infant blood groups differing does not automatically mean haemolytic disease.

What to do after the result

Ask who will review the result, when you will hear back, whether further tests are needed and exactly when to repeat it. Newborn follow-up may be needed within hours and must reflect the result and the baby’s condition, not a routine adult turnaround time. Prolonged neonatal jaundice, especially with pale stools or dark urine, needs assessment including the direct/conjugated fraction. Imaging is selected when liver, gallbladder or drainage disease is suspected; it does not exclude every possible cause.

Treatment targets the cause and severity. Most jaundiced babies can continue breastfeeding with effective feeding support; expressed milk, donor milk or formula may be needed individually. Do not withhold necessary supplementation or interrupt breastfeeding without a clinical plan. Some babies need monitored phototherapy, rarely urgent specialist treatment such as exchange transfusion. Feeds alone are not treatment for dangerous bilirubin levels, and sunlight, water or herbal remedies are not substitutes. Keep the written follow-up plan and seek help sooner if symptoms change.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Laboratory guidance uses bilirubin fractions, laboratory-specific intervals and clinical context; preparation and medicine changes require individual instructions.

Current neonatal guidance uses postnatal age, gestation, serum levels and risks, with prompt testing and coordinated follow-up rather than a universal newborn cutoff.

Feeding guidance distinguishes suboptimal intake from breast milk jaundice and supports ongoing breastfeeding plus supplementation or treatment when clinically needed.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to record the result, units, baby’s age at sampling, medicines, feeding observations and the team’s next appointment. A log cannot diagnose the cause, interpret treatment thresholds or decide that jaundice is safe. Do not delay urgent care to enter or compare numbers.

When to seek help

Obtain immediate emergency help for first-day jaundice or a jaundiced baby who is difficult to wake, not feeding, floppy or stiff, breathing badly, has no wet nappies or temperature at least 38°C or at most 36°C. Seek urgent same-day advice for suspected/worsening jaundice, dark urine or pale stools. New jaundice in older patients also needs urgent assessment. Do not fast babies, change medicines or replace prescribed treatment with home remedies.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A bilirubin result helps guide assessment; it does not diagnose the cause alone.
  • Preparation depends on the ordered tests. Do not fast a newborn or stop medicines on your own.
  • Newborn decisions require age in hours, gestation, serum results, risks and trends: not an adult range or one fixed cutoff.
  • Follow-up, feeding support and any treatment must match the individual; urgent symptoms override a routine test appointment.

Frequently asked questions

When is newborn jaundice dangerous?

First-day jaundice, rapid rises, haemolysis, infection or other illness need prompt assessment. A jaundiced baby who is difficult to wake, not feeding, floppy or stiff, breathing badly, has no wet nappies or a temperature at least 38°C or at most 36°C needs immediate emergency care. Do not wait for a bilirubin result.

Are there three types of newborn jaundice?

Physiological, suboptimal-intake and breast milk jaundice are useful patterns, not an exhaustive classification. Early low milk intake differs from later breast milk jaundice. Blood-cell, infection, liver and bile-duct causes must be considered when appropriate.

What can cause an abnormal result?

Excess red-cell breakdown, altered liver processing or blocked bile drainage can raise bilirubin. Examples include haemolytic disorders, hepatitis, cirrhosis, Gilbert syndrome, stones and strictures. The fractions and other findings guide further testing; one high result does not prove liver damage or cancer.

What happens after testing?

A clinician interprets the result, decides on further tests or imaging and sets a repeat-testing or treatment plan. Ask for the actual number, units, fractions and next contact time. Newborn follow-up may be much faster than routine adult results, and new symptoms need earlier help.

Must I fast or stop medicines?

Only follow specific instructions for your ordered tests and situation. There is no universal four-hour rule. Do not fast a newborn for a routine bilirubin check. Disclose all medicines and supplements, but do not stop prescribed treatment without advice.

Can a skin reading replace the blood test?

Sometimes it is useful for newborn screening, but babies in their first 24 hours or born before 35 weeks of gestation, and those with high or near-treatment readings, need blood testing according to the protocol. A colour estimate or home photograph cannot establish the bilirubin level.

Is one bilirubin number safe for every baby?

No. Age in hours, gestation, clinical condition, risks and the trend determine the assessment and treatment threshold. Use the clinician’s interpretation, not an adult reference range or a number from another baby.

Should breastfeeding stop if the baby is yellow?

Usually breastfeeding continues with support and assessment of effective intake. Extra expressed milk, donor milk or formula may be needed; interruption is rarely advised and needs a specific plan. Do not delay phototherapy or emergency care in favour of feeding alone.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
